place: A shelving shingle beach in a bay, at the time of the month when the tides are climbing toward springs, with an offshore breeze in the evenings.
things: the last tide line of wrack
the boat's painter, coiled in the bow and tied to nothing
the fisherman asleep in his cottage
outcome: The fisherman hauled the boat a boat's length above yesterday's wrack line and left the painter coiled, as he has all week. Tonight's tide is a hand higher than last night's and the one after higher still; on the second night the water reaches the stern, lifts it, and works the boat round and afloat at the top of the tide. The offshore breeze and the ebb take her out of the bay with the oars in her. By morning there is a keel mark that ends at the new wrack line and a boat that may fetch up miles down the coast, or on rocks, or nowhere.

outcome: An hour's raking where the signs are thick fills the basket; a few paces off the bed gives almost nothing. Cooked at once they open well and taste sweet but every mouthful grinds with sand. The ones left overnight in a bucket of clean seawater spit out their grit and are good eating next day. Any left in the bucket a second day in still water foul it and die, and a dead one cooked among the rest can make a person very ill; the ones that do not open in the pot, or gape before it, are the ones to throw out.

outcome: The walk round takes a quarter hour at low water. The player spends two hours in the cove; by then the flood has been running for three and the ledges at the point are under waist-deep surging water that would knock a person off their feet onto rock. The way back is shut and will stay shut for six or seven hours. The cliffs are rotten and unclimbable. The back of the cove stays dry on this tide, so it is a cold, hungry, frightening wait into the dark rather than a drowning, but on a spring tide with a swell that strip goes under too.

outcome: Two gallons of seawater hold about half a pound of salt, and getting it means boiling away all two gallons: three or four hours of hard fire and an armful of wood every quarter hour. It works, but the yield looks pitiful for the labour. Boiled right down to dryness the salt is grey, damp-drawing and bitter from the last liquor; taken off while still a wet slush and drained in a cloth, it is whiter and sweeter but there is less of it. The pot is left with a hard scale burnt to its bottom and will rust by morning if not scoured and greased.

outcome: One gull sidles in, takes a herring and gets away with it; its cries and the flash of fish bring twenty more within a minute. place: An open sandy beach backed by dunes, facing the winter gales, where old people say a ship was lost in their grandparents' time.
things: black oak ribs of an old wreck

outcome: The gale's waves drag sand off the beach and lay it on bars offshore, dropping the beach level by a man's height in three days. Where there was smooth sand there is now a bed of clay with a row of black ribs standing out of it and the fluke of an anchor. Villagers come and saw off what oak they can and dig for anything iron, but the anchor is heavier than four men can shift and the tide gives them only a few hours each low water. Through the next weeks of gentle swell the sand walks back up the beach, and within a month or two everything is buried again as if it had never been.

outcome: The small silver-grey sticks from above the highest tide line are bone dry and catch quickly, burning fast, hot and spitting, with salt colouring the flame. The big log from the fresh tide line is soaked through and only hisses, smokes and half-smothers the fire it is put on; it would need weeks above the tides to be any use. So the fire eats armfuls of small stuff and needs feeding every few minutes. In the wind it throws sparks downwind that pinhole the cloak, and unless it is set in a scrape or behind stones most of its heat blows away.

outcome: The crew leave the wet net in a heap, meaning to spread it in the morning, and then weather and other work keep them ashore a week. Inside the heap the twine stays wet and warm; the slime rots, the heap heats a little and stinks, and the hemp goes soft and brown through the middle while the outside, which dried, looks well enough. At the next shot the net comes up heavy with herring and tears open along a whole fathom, spilling most of the catch. Mending it takes two people two days, and the rotted twine around the mend will go next.

place: A sheltered harbour with warm summer water, where boats either lie afloat on moorings all season or are hauled out on the hard between trips.
things: an oak-planked boat left afloat from spring to autumn, her bottom bare of tar since last year
a sister boat hauled out every week and tarred in spring

outcome: Through the summer shipworm larvae settle on the bare bottom of the moored boat and bore in through pinholes too small to notice, then eat along inside the planks, never breaking the surface. By autumn she looks sound, leaks a little more than she did, and a spike pushed at a garboard plank goes in to the hilt: the wood inside is a honeycomb of chalk-lined tubes. Three planks must be replaced before winter or she will open up in the first hard sea. The tarred boat that dried out weekly has no worm at all, because worm dies when the wood dries and cannot get through tar.

outcome: A limpet that has been touched clamps down, and then nothing a person has will shift it: fingers slide off, and a knife worked under the rim snaps its tip or chips the shell to pieces before the animal lets go. An unwarned limpet, sitting slightly raised, comes off whole with one sharp sideways knock from a heel or a stone. So the first ones the player tries are all failures and the knife is the worse for it, and after that a meal's worth, thirty or forty, takes a quarter hour. They are tough, and need long stewing or a hard pounding before they are eaten.

place: A flat sandy beach at dead low water, the sea two hundred paces off, with a heavy larch-on-oak fishing boat lying on her bilge where the last tide left her.

outcome: One person cannot drag this boat: she weighs as much as a carthorse and her keel cuts into the sand. Levering the bow up with an oar and getting round poles under the keel lets her be shoved a length at a time, fetching each freed pole round to the front, but on soft sand the poles sink and it is an hour's brutal work to gain thirty paces, and the oar may crack. The sea will do the job free: in about three hours the tide reaches her and lifts her. The sensible thing is to carry the anchor down-beach, bed it, and wait, so that she does not float off untended.

outcome: The knife left on the thwart wet with fish blood and seawater has a brown bloom by the next morning. In three days the edge is pitted and it is rusted to a rough orange all over; in three weeks the blade is scaly, the tang has swelled and split the wooden handle, and it will never take a fine edge again. The oiled knife in its greased sheath is bright all season. Scouring the neglected one with wet sand and an hour on the whetstone gets a usable knife back if it is caught in the first week, thinner than before.

outcome: Rain that falls on dunes sinks in and floats as a thin lens on the salt water beneath. A hole dug in the hollow behind the first dune ridge reaches damp sand at arm's depth and, a little below that, slowly seeps a few cupfuls of cloudy water that tastes flat, faintly brackish and drinkable. Dug deeper to get more, the hole breaks into the salt beneath and what rises is undrinkable, and the hole is spoiled. Dug too near the beach, it is salt from the start. The sides slump in unless the hole is wide, and it refills only a few cups an hour.

outcome: Digging forty lugworm and baiting and staking the line takes most of the low water. The tide covers it for eight or nine hours and the player can do nothing but wait and not be late back. outcome: The shrimper treads on the buried fish, which raises its spines and does not move away. The pain is immediate and out of all proportion to the pinprick: within minutes the foot is swollen and he is sick and sweating with it, and it gets worse for the first half hour. He drops the net and must hobble a furlong to the fire with the tide coming in behind him. Holding the foot in water as hot as he can bear breaks the pain within a quarter hour; without that it rages for a couple of hours and aches for a day. No lasting harm, but the day's shrimping is over and the net may be floating off. Shod or shuffling feet would have prevented it.
